introduction-why-total-spend-is-a-useles.core: Total cloud spend going up says nothing about efficiency on its own. If customers grew faster than cost, you got more efficient. Value is judged by cost per unit of business output.

first_principles.problem: The bill jumps 50% and leadership demands cuts, even though usage doubled and cost per customer actually fell.
truths: Cost scales with usage.
Growth naturally raises spend.
Efficiency is a ratio, not a total.
derivation: Celebrate a falling unit cost even when the total rises.

analogy.title: A grocery bill for a growing family
analogy.story: The bill doubled, but the family went from 2 to 5 people, so the cost per person fell.
analogy.breaks: Unit cost ignores absolute affordability. You still need budgets.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The conversation moves from panic to insight.

check.q: Can rising cloud spend be good news?
check.a: Yes, if business output (customers, transactions) grew faster, so unit cost fell.

defining-unit-economics-in-the-cloud.core: Unit economics divides cloud cost by a unit of business output (cost per order, per active user, per GB processed), linking engineering spend directly to value delivered.

first_principles.problem: Engineers see dollars and resources while the business sees customers and revenue, with no shared metric.
truths: Every product has a core output.
Cost drivers can be mapped to outputs.
Shared metrics align teams.
derivation: Choose a **unit** that reflects value (an order, a stream minute).

analogy.title: Miles per gallon
analogy.story: A car's fuel spend matters less than how far each gallon takes you.
analogy.breaks: A bad unit choice (one that doesn't drive cost) gives misleading signals.

example.title: An e-commerce platform

steps.label: Use
steps.detail: Each architecture change is judged by its effect on $/order.

example.outcome: a shared language for engineering and finance.

check.q: What makes a good unit for unit economics?
check.a: A measure of business output that actually drives cloud cost and reflects value.

the-hierarchy-of-units-choosing-the-righ.core: Unit metrics range from infrastructure (cost per vCPU-hour) to service (cost per API request) to business (cost per customer, per dollar of revenue). Pick the level that suits the audience and the decision.

first_principles.problem: Showing executives $/vCPU-hour, or showing engineers $/revenue, doesn't help either make decisions.
truths: Different audiences control different levers.
Lower-level metrics are easier to measure.
Higher-level metrics show business impact.
derivation: **Business**: $/customer, cloud cost as % of revenue, for executives.
**Roll up** from lower levels to higher ones.

analogy.title: A restaurant's numbers
analogy.story: The chef tracks cost per ingredient, the manager cost per dish, and the owner food cost as a % of revenue.
analogy.breaks: Rolling up requires good allocation; shared costs blur the picture.

example.title: One dashboard, three views

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each audience sees what it can act on.

example.outcome: metrics drive the right decisions at each level.

check.q: Which unit metric suits a CFO?
check.a: A business-level metric such as cloud cost as a percentage of revenue, or cost per customer.

calculating-the-unit-cost-in-practice.core: The numerator (cost) needs accurate allocation, including shared costs. The denominator (units) needs business data joined to the same time window. Getting both right is the real work.

first_principles.problem: Untagged resources and shared clusters make the cost side wrong, and the unit counts live in another team's database.
truths: Allocation quality determines numerator accuracy.
Units come from product analytics or billing.
Time windows must align.
derivation: **Numerator**: tagged direct cost + a fair share of shared costs.
**Automate** it in a pipeline and dashboard.

analogy.title: Calculating cost per loaf in a bakery
analogy.story: You need the flour per loaf (direct) and a share of oven electricity and rent (shared), divided by loaves sold that month.
analogy.breaks: Perfect accuracy is unattainable, but consistency matters more than precision for trends.

check.q: What are the two practical challenges in unit cost calculation?
check.a: Accurately allocating cost (the numerator, including shared costs) and getting matching business unit counts (the denominator).

margins-analysis-connecting-unit-cost-to.core: Unit cost feeds gross margin: revenue per unit minus cost per unit (including cloud COGS). Engineering choices that reduce unit cost directly raise margin and company valuation.

first_principles.problem: Engineers don't see how architecture choices affect profitability, so cost work feels optional.
truths: Cloud spend for serving customers is COGS.
Gross margin drives valuation, especially for SaaS.
Small per-unit savings compound at scale.
derivation: Cloud **serving cost** is part of COGS.
Compare **revenue per unit vs cost per unit**.

analogy.title: A lemonade stand
analogy.story: If each cup sells for $1 and the lemons cost $0.40, every cent saved on lemons is pure profit.
analogy.breaks: Not all cloud spend is COGS. R&D environments are OpEx, not cost of sales.

example.title: A SaaS plan's margins

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Eight margin points from engineering work.

example.outcome: engineers see cost work as profit work.

check.q: Why is reducing cloud cost per customer valuable to a SaaS company?
check.a: It raises gross margin, which directly influences profitability and valuation multiples.

diseconomies-of-scale-when-growth-makes-.core: Good architectures get cheaper per unit as they grow. Poor ones get more expensive: N² communication, unbounded data retention, noisy-neighbour over-provisioning or per-tenant infrastructure all make unit cost rise with scale.

first_principles.problem: As customers double, cost triples. Growth is making the business less profitable.
truths: Some costs grow faster than linearly.
Fixed costs amortise as you grow; superlinear costs compound.
Rising unit cost is an early warning sign.
derivation: Find **superlinear drivers** (cross-AZ chatter, full scans, retention).

analogy.title: A party where everyone must greet everyone
analogy.story: 10 guests make 45 handshakes; 100 guests make 4,950. The effort per guest rises with the size of the crowd.
analogy.breaks: Some rise during growth is investment (new regions), so separate it from inefficiency.

check.q: What's a classic architectural cause of diseconomies of scale?
check.a: For example, all-to-all (N²) service communication, or unbounded data retention.

engineering-proxies-when-you-dont-have-b.core: When revenue or customer data isn't available, use engineering proxies that track business activity (requests, active sessions, jobs processed, GB ingested) to compute meaningful unit costs.

first_principles.problem: Platform teams can't access the CRM or finance data, so they skip unit economics entirely.
truths: Technical activity correlates with business activity.
Telemetry is already available to engineers.
An imperfect proxy beats no metric.
derivation: Choose a **proxy correlated with value** (requests ≈ usage).
**Validate the correlation** with business data later.

analogy.title: Using footfall to estimate a shop's sales
analogy.story: Without the till data, door counts still tell you a lot.
analogy.breaks: Proxies can diverge, for example bots inflating requests, so sanity-check them.

example.title: Cost per 1M API requests

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Releases that degrade efficiency are spotted immediately.

example.outcome: unit economics without waiting for perfect data.

check.q: Give an example of an engineering proxy for business output.
check.a: For example, API requests served, active sessions, or jobs processed.
